Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO after a second affair came to light. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.
Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future after reports emerged of a second extramarital affair — this time with an employee.
In a statement issued on Thursday morning, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.
The New York Times first reported on the latest scandal, alleging that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.
Both are married; Huang tied the knot with his wife Lori in 1985.
The latest revelation emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China . The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.
The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.
Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.
Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.
While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.
According to The Wall Street Journal , Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.
Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.
Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.
Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.
Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Still, Nvidia's stock hit all-time highs only a month ago, as US technology giants kept announcing billions in spending on AI infrastructure.
Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales. — meaning demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.
"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank
Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.
His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.
Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.
Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.
Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.
Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.
He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.
Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.
At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.
Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.
China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.
While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.
Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.
The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips .
However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.
Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.
Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.
The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

If you’re hoping to cut your cell phone bill by switching providers and maybe get a new device as a carrot, check out Mint Mobile right now. To get the deal, you will need to sign up for a 12-month unlimited plan for $180, which breaks down to $15 a month. (Mint requires full payment up front, plus taxes and fees.) Another catch? The unlimited plan also throttles down speeds after 50 GB per month, but it includes 20 GB for hot spot connections. Mint will offer an additional credit of $400 or more when you trade in an eligible unlocked phone (iPhone 16 or higher, Galaxy S25 or higher, Z Flip7 or Fold7 or higher, or Pixel 10 or higher).
Mint rarely offers deals or coupons because its plans are priced lower than traditional carriers, and you would have to pay full price for a new phone; while you’ll still have to shell out to cover the balance for the device, it is still more economical than the phone deals offered by the big carriers.
For more savings, check out the best Early Black Friday deals we are following.

Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.
The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.
Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".
Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.
Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.
Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.
Pictures showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics
The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.
In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.
Other footage shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by an explosion.
The hospital's director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, later told a news conference that Israeli forces had fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building but that only one exploded.
"What's happened in Nasser Medical Complex is targeting the health sector mainly. We are talking about doctors, we are talking about civilians, we are talking about patients," he said.
"Also, there is... huge damage [to] the infrastructure inside the hospital."
Footage filmed by a freelance journalist working for the BBC showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics, as well as hallways and lifts.
News agencies also published photos that appeared to show an unexploded missile.
Photographs appeared to show an unexploded missile inside Nasser hospital's surgical building
Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who was wounded in the head, said he and other medical staff had just finished work around 00:30 and had been preparing to go to sleep when there was an explosion.
"My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told the BBC.
"I started struggling to free myself and started calling out, 'Guys! Guys!' I began crawling, trying to pull my leg out from beneath the rubble. I managed to pull myself free. It was dark, there were no lights, nothing at all."
He said he had been lying in a bed near Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who was killed. Another colleague suffered a broken leg.
"Dr Rizq was the kindest person in this department. He was very kind and always willing to help... And of course, he was a surgeon, one of the best among us."
He added: "Patients were killed as well. There were patients in the rooms next to us who were killed. A patient comes to the hospital seeking treatment and leaves carried on people's shoulders. I do not know what kind of humanity this is."
Gaza's health ministry said surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira was among those killed
The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital.
"The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.
The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.
A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known".
"The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.
However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.
Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths.
"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.
Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza.
Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp.
The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City.
Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.
More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, greets Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, right, and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, center, during their meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, Moscow, Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP hide caption
MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.
The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.
Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.
Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, second right, speaks to U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, second left, and Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, third left, as Russian Presidential foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, behind Putin, and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Special Presidential Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries Kirill Dmitriev, right, sit near during the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin, in Moscow, on Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP hide caption
But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.
Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow.
Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said.
He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks during a press conference after a bilateral meeting with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Wednesday, ahead of the European Political Community Summit. Virginia Mayo/AP hide caption
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.
Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal.
"The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday.
He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.
Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.
Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."
Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.
Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.
Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.
Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.
Law enforcement officer inspects the site of a car explosion that killed a military serviceman in St. Petersburg, Russia, Thursday. AP hide caption
A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's main criminal investigation agency. It didn't identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.
Several senior Russian military officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

The baby’s father said he died of hypothermia overnight in their family’s tent in southern Gaza.
A Palestinian infant has died from the cold in a tent sheltering his displaced family in southern Gaza, his father and a doctor said, as Israel continues to impose severe restrictions on winter supplies to the war-ravaged territory.
Nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq “died from hypothermia” in Khan Younis, in the southern region of the enclave, a doctor who spoke on he condition of anonymity told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Ahmed Raqiq, the baby’s father, told AFP that Kinan died after cold temperatures hit Gaza overnight.
“I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser Hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death,” he said.
“I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in a burial shroud,” he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet.
Gaza’s Civil Defence spokesman, Mahmoud Basal, confirmed the infant’s death after exposure to extreme cold, Palestinian news network Al-Quds reported.
The death comes as the United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan led a coalition of more than 50 countries and organisations calling on Israel to provide immediate entry of critical items for shelter, fuel, water, sanitation and health to Gaza.
With winter arriving, the group said, “far too many people in Gaza are still without adequate shelter, and risk exposure to hypothermia, respiratory infections, waterborne diseases and other preventable illnesses”.
The statement echoed recent criticism of Israel over its restrictions by the United States-led Board of Peace and United Nations humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher.
Responding to the Board of Peace, Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel had allowed in supplies including 91,000 tents and that “Hamas alone is responsible for the suffering of the people of Gaza.”
As well as the cold, Gaza has experienced flooding this week following heavy rains, affecting tens of thousands of people’s tents. Five people, including three children, died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment eroded and collapsed onto their tents.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms.
Around 65 percent of Gaza’s people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said.
James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season.
“It’s very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It’s not yet winter,” Elder said.
“We’re weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold.”

Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets
Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.
These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.
The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.
Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.
Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.
Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.
Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.
He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.
Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.
Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.
Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Sepahvand, Manesh and Noori had claimed asylum in the UK and received temporary leave to remain. None of them had regular full-time employment.
It is understood they met by chance and were then directed by Sepahvand and his contacts in Iran. There appeared to be no evidence of any wider plot.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh before sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

Maryland Democrat challenges party leader after midterms sweep, saying: ‘The American people called for change’
Chris Van Hollen, the Democratic senator of Maryland, announced on Thursday that he is challenging Chuck Schumer for the role of Senate majority leader when Democrats regain the chamber’s majority in January.
“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement posted on social media.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
Schumer, the leader of the Democratic minority in the current Senate, responded less than a minute later in a social media post of his own. “I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together – 55 seats and counting is an amazing result – and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
The battle pits a progressive Democrat, Van Hollen, against a centrist, Schumer.
Van Hollen’s challenge comes after he said he was considering a bid and after Schumer said he had the necessary support to win. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
The race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades. The question of whether to re-elect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators will not say publicly how they will vote. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election, and Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them. But some of the winning candidates, most notably Michigan’s senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed, did not initially have Schumer’s support.
Schumer has been talking to Democratic senators since the election about forming an agenda for 2027.
“I’m going to win it,” Schumer told the Associated Press in an interview last week.

İrlanda Başbakanı Micheal Martin, AB Konseyi Başkanı Antonio Costa ve İsviçre Konfederasyonu Başkanı Guy Parmelin, İrlanda'nın başkenti Dublin'de düzenlenen Avrupa Siyasi Topluluğu (AST) 9. Zirvesi'nin ardından ortak basın toplantısı düzenledi.
Costa, basın toplantısında, zirvede ana temanın Ukrayna'da adil ve kalıcı barış sağlanması arayışı olduğunu söyledi.
Avrupa'nın müzakerelerdeki önceliğinin ateşkes, Karadeniz'de seyrüsefer serbestisi ve barış anlaşması için gerekli koşulların sağlanması olduğunu dile getiren Costa, Rusya'nın barışa hazır olduğuna yönelik hiçbir işaret vermediğini öne sürdü.
Costa, Rusya-Ukrayna Savaşı'nın sona erdirilmesi için diplomatik çabaların arttığını kaydederek, Avrupa'da güvenliğin yeniden tesis edilmesini sağlayacak barışın net ilkelere dayanması gerektiğini vurguladı.
Ukrayna'nın kendi geleceğini özgürce seçebilmesi, kıta güvenliğinin geleceği konusunda Avrupa'nın masada bulunması ve Avrupa güvenlik mimarisinin 1975 Helsinki Nihai Senedi'nde değinilen esaslara dayalı olması gerektiğini ifade eden Costa, "Kendi güvenliğimizin Ukrayna'nın güvenliğinden geçtiği açıktır. Ukrayna'ya desteğimizi sürdüreceğiz." dedi.
Costa, müzakerelerde Avrupa'yı kimin temsil etmesi gerektiğine yönelik soru üzerine, çeşitli konularda Avrupa adına görüşme yapacak doğru kişilerin bulunduğunu söyledi.
Toprak konusunda Ukrayna'nın, ülkenin Birliğe katılımı gibi konularda AB'nin, güvenlik garantileri hakkında da Gönüllüler Koalisyonu ülkelerinin konuşmasının normal olduğunu belirten Costa, müzakerelere girişmeye hazır olduklarını kaydetti.
İrlanda Başbakanı Martin, zirvedeki görüşmelerden dört temel sonucun çıktığına işaret ederek, bunları Ukrayna'ya sarsılmaz destek, hibrit tehditlerle mücadelede işbirliği, Avrupa'nın yenilikçilik kapasitesinin teknolojik gelişmelerle güçlendirilmesi ve temiz, uygun fiyatlı enerjiye erişimin sağlanması olarak sıraladı.
Zirvede Ukrayna'ya desteğin bir kez daha teyit edildiğini vurgulayan Martin, "Rusya'nın sivillere ve kritik altyapıya yönelik giderek yoğunlaşan saldırıları karşısında Ukrayna halkının cesaretini takdir ediyoruz." dedi.
Martin, Ukrayna'daki barış sürecinde ABD'nin rolüne ilişkin soruya verdiği yanıtta, Avrupa ülkelerinin Ukrayna'ya sağladığı mali, savunma ve askeri desteğin vazgeçilmez olduğunun altını çizdi.
Martin, Ukrayna Devlet Başkanı Volodimir Zelenskiy'nin hem ABD'nin hem de Rusya'nın Avrupa'nın katkısı olmadan Avrupa güvenliği ve savaşın uzun vadeli çözümü konusunda ilerleme sağlanamayacağını bildiğini dile getirdiğini aktardı.
Martin, "ABD'lilerin de müzakere masasında Avrupa'nın bir sesinin bulunması gerektiğini kabul edeceğini düşünüyorum." ifadesini kullandı.
İngiltere, Fransa ve Almanya öncülüğündeki "Gönüllüler Koalisyonu"nun gelecek hafta Almanya'nın başkenti Berlin'de yeniden toplanacağını kaydeden Martin, söz konusu girişimin Ukrayna'ya destek açısından önemli etkiler yarattığını söyledi.
Martin, Avrupa'nın demokratik süreçlerini hedef alan hibrit saldırılara da değinerek, bu saldırılarla kafa karışıklığı yaratmak, bölünmeleri körüklemek ve demokratik sistemlere duyulan güveni zayıflatmak isteyenler olduğunu belirtti.
Martin, "Başarılı olmalarına izin vermeyeceğiz. Demokrasilerimizi korumak için deneyimlerimizi paylaşmaya, birbirimizden öğrenmeye ve birlikte çalışmaya devam edeceğiz." dedi.
Konuşmasında enerji fiyatlarının düşürülmesi gerektiğini de vurgulayan Martin, fosil yakıtlardan uzaklaşılması, yenilenebilir enerji üretiminin artırılması, elektrik şebekeleri ile ülkeler arasındaki enerji bağlantılarının geliştirilmesinin daha güvenli ve uygun fiyatlı bir gelecek için önemli olduğunu ifade etti.
İsviçre Konfederasyonu Başkanı Parmelin, AST 9. Zirvesi sonrasında düzenlenen basın toplantısında konuştu.
Zirvenin, AST'nin kıta genelindeki liderler arasında diyalog ve fikir alışverişi için benzersiz bir platform sunduğunu bir kez daha kanıtladığına işaret eden Parmelin, "Jeopolitik gerilimlerin tırmandığı ve çok taraflı yapıların parçalandığı bir dönemde, bu platform her zamankinden daha büyük bir önem taşıyor." ifadesini kullandı.
Parmelin, başta Avrupa güvenliği ve rekabet gücünü artırmanın yolları olmak üzere bir dizi temel mesele üzerinde önemli görüşmeler gerçekleştirdiklerini kaydederek, bu fikir alışverişinin büyük bir değer taşıdığına işaret etti.
AST'nin, ortak sınamaları ele almalarına, işbirliğini güçlendirmelerine ve karşılıklı güveni daha da pekiştirmelerine olanak tanıdığına değinen Parmelin, şöyle konuştu:
"İsviçre, bu nedenle AST'ye özel bir değer atfetmekte ve topluluğun çalışmalarında aktif bir rol oynamaya kararlılıkla devam etmektedir. Bu doğrultuda, topluluğumuzun bir sonraki buluşmasına ev sahipliği yapmayı dört gözle bekliyoruz. AST'nin 10. Zirvesi, 15 Nisan 2027'de Zürih'te gerçekleştirilecek. Diyaloğu ve barışçıl işbirliğini teşvik etme konusundaki köklü geleneğimizden yola çıkarak AST'nin 10. Zirvesi'ne İsviçre’de ev sahipliği yapmaktan onur duyacağız."
Parmelin, AST'nin 10. Zirvesi'nde, önceki toplantılarda atılan adımların üzerine yenilerini ekleyeceklerini, ortak hedeflerini, Avrupa kıtası genelinde istikrar, güvenlik ve refaha yönelik somut işbirliğine dönüştürmeye gayret edeceklerini vurguladı.
"Avrupa'nın karşı karşıya olduğu sınamalar ulusal sınırlarla sınırlı değildir ve hiçbir ülke tek başına hareket ederek bu sorunların üstesinden gelemez." diyen Parmelin, Avrupa'nın kalbinde yer alan İsviçre'nin, uzun zamandır farklı bakış açılarının buluştuğu, görüş alışverişinde bulunduğu ve ortak bir payda arayışına girildiği bir merkez işlevi gördüğünü anımsattı.
Zürih'in, AST'nin tüm üyeleri arasında açık, yapıcı ve ileriye dönük tartışmalar için verimli bir ortam sağlayacağını umduklarının altını çizen Parmelin, "Avrupa için müreffeh ve barışçıl bir gelecek şekillendirme yönündeki ortak çabalarımızı sürdürmeyi ve AST ruhunu daha ileriye taşımayı dört gözle bekliyoruz." diye konuştu.

The battle pits a progressive Democrat, Van Hollen, against a centrist, Schumer, in the wake of Senate wins for progressive Democrats in Michigan and Maine who were not initially supported by Schumer.

Schumer is a cautious politician who has been widely criticized by Democratic voters for failing to stand up to Trump. Van Hollen, by contrast, took on the president’s mass deportation effort head on when he visited El Salvador in early 2025 and demanded to check on the condition of Kilmar Ábrego , a constituent who was wrongly deported to the country.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed , the Michigan Democrat who saw off Schumer’s preferred candidate in the primary, quickly endorsed Van Hollen.
Democrat Cindy Holscher has been elected Kansas’ next governor, narrowly defeating Republican Ty Masterson to keep the office in her party’s hands and extend a massive wave of Democratic victories across the country.
Taking time out of his busy schedule of posting on social media, Donald Trump sat down for a lengthy podcast interview with the sports pundit Stephen A Smith to express sympathy for Jensen Huang , who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees.
In the friendly, softball interview with Smith, Trump defended the Iran war with a big lie, and deflected blame for his party’s midterm losses with misinformation. An overnight Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians Thursday, including a teenage boy and a surgeon, medics said. Elsewhere in the devastated Palestinian territory, a nine-month-old baby died from the cold as families flee worsening flooding.

An Israeli air strike on southern Gaza's main hospital overnight killed at least six Palestinians including a surgeon and a teenage boy, medics said, the latest Israeli attack to undermine a year-old ceasefire in the ravaged territory.
The strike hit a building containing surgery wards at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis. Israel 's ​military alleged it had ‌targeted a senior Hamas commander and accused the militants of using the hospital complex to plan attacks, which ⁠the group denied.
Medics and witnesses said two missiles crashed through the roof of the five-storey building, causing extensive damage. The surgery department, which serves half of Gaza's 2 million people, was knocked out of service. ‌Twenty others were wounded.
Ayman Abu Obeid, a doctor who was wounded in the attack, said he was on ⁠an overnight shift in the hospital when an explosion ripped through the room where he and others were sleeping.
"All of a sudden the world turned upside down. It went dark all at once," he said from a hospital bed. Near him, piles ​of mangled furniture and medical equipment could be seen covered in dust from blown-out concrete. Torn wires hung down ‌from the ceiling.
Among those killed was Rezik Abushira, a surgeon who was featured in a 2026 documentary, "American Doctor" , working alongside three visiting US doctors who help provide medical care for Palestinians in Gaza.
The dead also included a 13-year-old boy, according to Gaza's education ministry.
Three more Palestinians were killed later on Thursday in separate ‌incidents. Two were killed and several wounded in an Israeli airstrike on a car in Gaza City, and one other person was killed by Israeli gunfire in central Gaza's Bureij refugee camp, medics said, ​taking Thursday's death toll to at least nine.
Commenting on the vehicle strike, the Israeli military said it hit a Hamas militant without giving further details. It did not comment on the other incident.
In a statement on the hospital strike, Israel's ​military said it targeted a person named Muhammad Abu Ismail, describing him as "the commander of Hamas' Khan Younis Brigade". The military alleged he and other ​militants "were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital".
The military accused the militants of "turning the Nasser Hospital compound into a ​headquarters and operating from there".
Hamas rejected the military's claim that it had used the hospital as a base for operations. It did not immediately comment on whether a leader from the group had ​been targeted, wounded or killed in the strike.
The Board of Peace , the body placed in charge of overseeing Gaza's ceasefire plan by US President Donald Trump , on Thursday called for the peace plan's immediate implementation.
"The tragic loss of life following an Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in Khan Younis underscores precisely why President Trump's Comprehensive Peace Plan must be implemented immediately without further delay," the Board said in a statement.
Israel's military has struck the Nasser Hospital complex at least seven times since the start of the Gaza war, hospital officials say.
Heavy rain last week flooded tens of thousands of people's tents in the Palestinian territory , where virtually the whole population has been displaced at least once by three years of Israeli bombardment.
Five people, including three children, died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment collapsed onto their tents.
A nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on Thursday, his father and a doctor told AFP.
The doctor, who saw the child and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq "died from hypothermia inside his family's displacement tent" in Khan Younis.
Ahmed Raqiq told AFP that his son Kinan died of cold during the night in their tent in southern Gaza.
"I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser hospital, but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death," he said.
"I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in burial shroud," he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet.
Read more Palestinians struggle to find food in Gaza a year after ceasefire
Hundreds of displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and central and northern areas of the territory after they were inundated by rainwater.
James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN children's agency, UNICEF , warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season.
"It's very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It's not yet winter," Elder said.
"We're weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold."
The UN 's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms.
Around 65 percent of Gaza's people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said.
Israel and Hamas declared a ceasefire on October 10, 2025 but Israel has kept striking the territory, vowing to kill anyone involved in the Hamas-led October 7 attack , the deadliest in Israel's history.

The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.
European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.
When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.
The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi , followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy .
Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.
Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine , alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.
"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.
But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.
Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.
"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."
Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.
"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.
European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.
Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.
Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden , could be among his demands.
"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."
This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of , especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.
"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"
US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."
Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.
They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.
The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.
Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.
Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.
But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru on Thursday, including people linked to the disbanded Sodalitium Christianae Vitae. The US-born pontiff also urged the Catholic Church to make amends to survivors and strengthen protections against abuse as he returned to the country where he served for nearly two decades.
Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru on Thursday, including some linked to the once-powerful and now-disbanded Catholic society, Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.
The US-born pope is on a nostalgic return to the nation he calls his "homeland", and knows the abuse scandal well from the nearly two decades he worked in Peru as a missionary and bishop.
Leo spent over an hour with the victims, meeting "each person individually, listening to their stories of suffering and their pain," and "thanked them for their invaluable testimony," the Vatican said.
Together, "they reflected on how to foster a shift in mindset – by listening to victims, seeking the truth, pursuing paths towards healing, and committing to the creation of safe environments," it said.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (SCV), a lay society founded in the 1970s that was widespread in Latin America, was shut down in 2025 by Leo's predecessor Francis after years of allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse, as well as corruption.
Before he was elected Pope Leo XIV , Robert Francis Prevost was the bishop designated to hear from SCV victims, who said he was supportive of their claims.
In an address to bishops earlier Thursday, Leo described the "pain" caused by Catholic clerical abuse and said the Church must make "amends" to victims and foster "a culture of prevention and protection."
Clerical abuse, a global scourge, was "a reality that has caused us so much pain," the 71-year-old said.
In April 2026, the Vatican announced plans to set up a "listening channel" in Lima for victims, and use assets seized from the lay movement to compensate them.
Renzo Orbegozo, a 50-year-old victim, told AFP they were seeking "comprehensive reparation."
"Many require psychological and medical support, as well as social reintegration – all of which, ultimately, translates into financial assistance," he said.
On the eve of the pope's South America tour, the US -based non-profit Bishop Accountability presented a list in Lima of 77 members of the Peruvian clergy it said had been publicly accused of abusing minors.
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the group, called on Leo to implement "zero tolerance" of abusers.
The head of the 1.4 billion Catholics has not shied away from tackling sensitive political and social topics during his three-nation Latin American tour.
Pilgrim Pedro Campos said Leo was "a member of our country who ... knows the needs of all Peruvians."
At a speech later to some 40,000 people on the challenges facing Peruvians, the pontiff slammed "machismo" attitudes and said violence against women was "a reality that wounds all of humanity."
There was no excuse for "an unequal sharing of domestic responsibilities or the subordination of one spouse to the other," he said.
Chicago-born Leo was given a raucous reception by crowds lining the streets, chanting his name.
Thousands of people – including children dressed as the pope or as bishops – lined up for a glimpse of the pope as he drove by in the popemobile.
At a prayer vigil attended by some 60,000 young people in Lima's national stadium, the pope made his way around on foot to greet people, as thousands held up their phones as torches.
The intense trip to Uruguay , Argentina and Peru comes just weeks after the pope had surgery for lung cancer, but he shows no sign of flagging.
In his speech, Leo made fond references to Peru's landscape and culture, telling the Catholic clergy to think of their mission as a difficult but rewarding walk, like the path that leads to Machu Picchu.
He compared the Catholic mission to the "steep ascents" of the Inca Trail in Peru.
The trail, an ancient network of routes that traverses much of the Andes, "is not to be walked alone," he cautioned.
Read more Pope Leo XIV returns to second homeland Peru and a nationwide welcome
During his tenure in Peru, Prevost worked in poor and remote northern areas, and remained close to local communities during periods of hardship, visiting them sometimes on horseback.
Six days in Peru will see Leo travel from the deep Amazon to the high Andes. He will visit Cuzco, at more than 3,400 metres (11,000 feet) elevation, which will test his recovery from lung surgery.
He will also make an emotional return to Chiclayo, the northern city where he was bishop for a decade.

Reports of alleged incident follow US envoys’ meetings with the Russian and Ukrainian president.
Finland’s military says its forces have detected a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised mediation efforts led by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
A spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said in an email to the Reuters news agency that its forces “detected … a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation”, adding that Finland is not under “any immediate military threat”.
The statement did not provide further details on where the strike originated, the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected.
Reuters said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused Wednesday’s strike.
Estonia shares a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea with Finland. Local media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship which had returned to Saint Petersburg after the alleged attack.
Ukraine’s Security Service has said it carried out the attack, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. In recent days, Russia said it had intercepted at least 146 Ukrainian drones in the northwestern Leningrad region.
On Wednesday, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO warplanes were scrambled in response.
On Thursday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland.
The US shuttle diplomacy followed trilateral negotiations in the United Arab Emirates this week, which produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners .
Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported that the prisoner exchange should happen in two to three weeks. If finalised, it would be the latest in a long line of such exchanges.
“We are also working toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families,” Kushner said on X on Thursday, following his meetings.
texts.https://www.dw.com/en/what-have-the-talk:
The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?
The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine , the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.
"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin .
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.
Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."
Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.
"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.
Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."
A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea , who have been held in Russian prisons for years.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.
"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.
Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.
"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."
Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.
She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.
Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.
"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel ," the political scientist says.
Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist , for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."
Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.
"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.
The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.
In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.
"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.
The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.
Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.
"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.
Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.
The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating , only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.
Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.
Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.
Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

William, 17, says ‘nights were pretty cold’ and he ‘honestly didn’t think’ he’d survive
A teenage boy who survived almost a week lost in dense Australian bushland sang John Denver’s Take Me Home, Country Roads as he held out hope of rescue on long nights alone in the wilderness.
William, whose surname has been withheld, was dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend in Victoria’s east last Friday.
The 17-year-old was reported missing at about 4pm that day after failing to return from a trip to retrieve further camping equipment. He was wearing only shorts and work boots and had left his phone, food supplies and water behind.
After an extensive operation of more than 100 people, including the police dog and rescue squads, the police air wing found William on Thursday morning lying down in a creek near Walhalla, 130km east of Melbourne.
He lost his way after taking a wrong turn on a track, and later slipped and fell down a cliff.
He told Seven’s Sunrise program John Denver’s country classic, which repeats the line “take me home, to the place I belong”, was a childhood favourite of his that brought him solace as he braved harsh conditions and loneliness.
“It’s a good childhood song of mine. It brings me great comfort,” he said from his hospital bed in Traralgon on Friday morning. “I started doing it one night, made me feel OK, so I just kept doing it.”
William shared an emotional reunion with his mother, Elizabeth Barkley, soon after being rescued. She told reporters on Thursday between tears that she was “over the moon” and he was “never leaving the house again”.
William told Sunrise their warm embrace was the “best moment of my life”.
“I think she’s going to stand true with that comment,” he said with a laugh. “She’s giving me a firm look from across the room at the moment, so not expecting to go out any time soon.”
William said he was “doing great” after enjoying a “great sleep” in a “comfy bed” on Thursday night and “finally getting some food into me”.
“I’m over the moon to be safe,” he said. “The nights were pretty cold. I think a couple of times it was raining. Hot days, so I got a bit sunburnt, pretty treacherous surroundings.
After seeing the helicopter flying overhead, William, who was sheltering on a rock under towels and heavily sunburnt, gave a wave and fist-bump before being airlifted to safety. He said he was feeling “pure euphoria”.
“Just happiness and gratefulness that a moment that I thought might never happen, has happened, and I am finally going to see my mum again,” he said.
“There were a few times were I’m thinking ‘geez, it’s getting dark out here, I don’t know if they’re going to see me’.”
William got by on a packet of chicken-flavoured chips, which he rationed over several days. He said he also drank water from the creek that he was sheltering by.
“Last night I had dinner … and I had some Macca’s, which was good, so I got plenty of food in,” he said. “I’m super grateful for all the paramedics and nurses, search and rescue … everyone that was involved.”
Pilot Dave Wylie told reporters it had been an incredibly challenging search for crews and it was lucky William was sheltering in an open area.
“A lot of the areas are so thick that you can’t actually see the forest floor so even if someone was there, potentially you could fly right past them,” he said.
“If he wasn’t in the open area like he was, we absolutely could have flown right past him without seeing him.”
William was being transported to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne for further observation and testing by specialists, after suffering from dehydration. He was in a stable condition on Friday afternoon.
Barkley told Nine’s A Current Affair she was in awe as to how well her son had handled days alone in the bush.
“I just couldn’t believe he survived that long,” she said. “But he’s a footballer. He’s tough, he’s very, very fit.
Barkley said William had missed a turn on a track and became lost on Friday and curled up under some bushes when it got dark.
“I had instinct … I knew he was still alive,” she said of the following days. “I knew in my heart … And I was just praying, and praying, and praying.”

US Senator Chris Van Hollen has said he is running for Senate majority leader as Democrats gear up to take charge of the US Congress in January following a Democratic landslide in this month’s midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a post on X late on Thursday that Americans had “called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption”.
“To deliver, we need new leadership,” he said, adding that “this isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call”.
Van Hollen has faced mounting calls to enter the race for Senate majority leader amid growing opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ‘s continued tenure after he faced criticism over how he has handled the Democratic caucus during the Trump presidency.
US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan was the first to back Van Hollen’s decision to run. In a post on X, El-Sayed said: “I called on Sen. Chris Van Hollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.”
“We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed said.
On Thursday, Democratic Party leaders gathered in Denver, Colorado, for a two-day conference on the future of the party, following the sweeping victories in the midterms.
Some progressives at the conference have argued that it is time to change the direction and the leadership of the Democratic Party.
“[Chuck] Schumer has spent nearly 50 years in elected office,” said Washington, DC-based political commentator and strategist James Butler, adding that while he respected the US senator’s service, “it is time for veteran Democrats to make space for younger, more energetic members”.
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has repeatedly challenged Washington’s relationship with Middle Eastern partners.
Van Hollen, the son of a US diplomat, has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “ chronic liar “, previously telling Al Jazeera the US-Israel war on Iran “is making America and our allies less safe”.
He also attempted to push forward legislation in Congress that would have required the Trump administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention.
This week, Van Hollen and 10 Senate colleagues urged congressional leaders to remove provisions from the annual defence policy bill that would expand weapons development and intelligence sharing with Israel.

IRGC claims Bahrain radar strike is a response to attacks on Iranian telecom tower in southern Hormozgan province.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.
The claim came hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing official sources, reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday.
In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC called the strike a “serious warning” to the “aggressor enemy” to stop what it said was a series of aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” the statement said.
The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said the IRGC’s Aerospace Force had “targeted and destroyed” the radar installation.
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet.
According to the Reuters news agency, it is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.
The claim comes as Israel’s security cabinet has ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran , according to Israeli media, including the public broadcaster KAN.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that if the US launches another war, every military base involved, anywhere from West Asia to Europe, would be a legitimate target for Iranian strikes.
US President Donald Trump has said he is prepared to return to war if the diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to deliver a deal.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has said economic pressure on Iran is working well enough that resuming large-scale military operations is unnecessary.
In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Iran’s parliament speaker and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would never go back to how it was before the war, and that “the ball is now in the American court “.
Meanwhile, US Central Command says its forces are still strictly enforcing the naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
